title: Module 1: Trust the Bike — Stack Check

blocks.content: You have practiced four tools so far: heavy feet and quiet hands, the hip hinge, pressure notes, and looking far enough ahead to choose a line. Use these questions to decide what to practice next.

blocks.question: You enter a rough section and feel yourself bracing on the bars. What can you adjust?

options.text: Soften your elbows and grip, let your feet support you, and slow if you need more control
Release the bars entirely
Lock your elbows so the front wheel cannot move
Accelerate to skim over the bumps

blocks.explanation: Keep both hands securely on the bars while allowing your arms and legs to move. Choose a slower pace whenever the bike feels hard to control.

blocks.question: Your hands begin to tingle on a rough ride. What is the useful response?

options.text: Stop somewhere safe, change hand position or pressure, and check bike fit if it continues
Ignore it because numbness is normal
Release your fingers from the bars on rough ground
Assume tire pressure is the only cause

blocks.explanation: Tingling is a cue to ease your grip and reassess comfort and fit. Persistent numbness deserves a qualified bike-fit or medical assessment.

blocks.question: What's the primary decoupling joint between upper and lower body on gravel?

options.text: Knees — they flex to absorb bumps
Shoulders — they float above the terrain
Hips — the hip hinge separates a stable lower body from a floating upper body
Elbows — bent elbows are the primary suspension

blocks.explanation: The Hip Hinge is the decoupling joint. Road cycling trains your body as a single rigid unit — stiff core, locked hips, power from glutes. Gravel demands two separate systems: a stable lower body driving the pedals, and a loose upper body absorbing terrain independently. The hips are where the separation happens.

blocks.question: On a familiar rough section, your head and shoulders feel rigid. What can you try?

options.text: Slow down and allow your hips, knees, and elbows to move while keeping a secure hold
Ride faster until the vibration disappears
Look only at the front tire
Lock your hips and shoulders together

blocks.explanation: The hip hinge is one way to let the bike move beneath you. Reduce pace first if you cannot see or steer clearly.

blocks.question: Your bike feels harsh and deflects on familiar gravel. What should you check before changing tire pressure?

options.text: Tire and rim limits, tire size, load, surface, and whether another setup issue is present
Whether the tire makes a particular pitch of buzz
A universal pressure number for all riders
How low a pressure you can reach before a rim strike

blocks.explanation: Noise alone does not diagnose pressure. Record the setup and compare one small change on a familiar route within manufacturer limits.

blocks.question: The course is wet after rain. How should you choose tire pressure?

options.text: Start within tire and rim limits, assess the actual surface, and compare small changes only in a safe setting
Always subtract 5 PSI from yesterday’s setting
Always add 5 PSI for wet gravel
Use the lowest pressure the gauge can show

blocks.explanation: Rain does not imply one universal PSI adjustment. Surface, tire, rim, load, and setup all matter. Slow down on reduced or uncertain grip.

blocks.question: Where should you look while approaching a rough section?

options.text: Far enough ahead to choose a visible line, with brief checks of the near surface as needed
At a fixed point exactly five seconds away
Only at the front wheel
At the rider ahead instead of the road

blocks.explanation: Look where you plan to go while keeping nearby hazards in view. Distance changes with speed, visibility, and terrain.

blocks.question: A rock appears close ahead on a descent. What matters most?

options.text: Keep steering and braking smooth, use the open space you can see, and slow if needed
Jerk the bars sharply around it
Trust peripheral vision to steer around it without looking
Hold the same speed to preserve balance

blocks.explanation: A close obstacle leaves little room for a big correction. Prioritize a controlled line and a manageable speed; practice scanning earlier on a safe route.

blocks.content: If you got 6 or more correct, your Trust stack is solid. You've internalized the foundation: weight through the pedals, hips as the hinge, pressure dialed, eyes ahead. Welcome to Module 2: Control the Inputs.
